D018-D001_h001.question:
I’ve always been kind of scattered, even as a kid. Teachers used to say I was “bright but away with the fairies.” I couldn’t sit still in class, missed instructions, lost my homework, and at home I’d start chores and then wander off and forget what I was doing. That never really went away. Even before I married, I’d double‑book myself, forget appointments, jump from one thing to another. Now, at 74, I still misplace my glasses three times a day and have trouble following a conversation or a TV plot if anything else is going on. My mind jumps around, and it feels like it’s always been that way.

The trauma came much later, when my husband died suddenly about ten years ago. Since then I sometimes get these sudden, vivid flashes of that night, like it’s replaying. I keep thinking I should have noticed something, that it’s partly my fault. I feel on edge a lot, easily startled, and when something spooks me, my heart races and it takes a long time to settle. I’ve pulled back from friends and church groups, and I spend more time alone than I used to. My head often feels foggy, but the trouble focusing has been there my whole life, long before he died.
D018-D001_h001.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

D018-D001_h002.question:
I’m 44 now, but this stuff goes way back. My teachers were already complaining in primary school that I “drifted off” and couldn’t sit still. I remember staring out the window instead of finishing worksheets, losing track of instructions halfway through. That’s kind of how it’s always been: I misplace drawings at work, forget where I put my keys or my phone, start an email and get distracted mid-sentence. It’s not new; it’s just more obvious now that my projects are complex.

The trauma came much later, after a car accident about three years ago. Since then, if I hear screeching brakes or see a crash scene in a movie, my chest tightens and I feel like I’m right back there. Sudden movements in my peripheral vision make me jump; I’m on edge a lot of the time. I keep thinking I should’ve seen the other car, that I could’ve prevented it somehow, and that thought just loops. I used to really enjoy sketching for fun or going out with friends, but I don’t feel much interest now. There’s this constant low-level fear and tension sitting in the background.
D018-D001_h002.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

D018-D001_h003.question:
I’m 44 now, but I’ve always been this way. Even in primary school my teachers told my mum I was “bright but scattered” and “never in my seat.” I’d start reading about, say, ancient ceramics and then realize an hour later I’d drifted off, reorganizing my pens or staring out the window. That same restless, jumpy focus has followed me into my job at the museum—I’ll be halfway through writing a catalog entry and suddenly I’m doing three other things and forgot what I was saying.

The trauma stuff came much later. A few years ago I was assaulted walking home. Since then, if someone brushes past me unexpectedly in a gallery, my whole body jolts; I overreact to the slightest touch. Sometimes, especially when I’m shelving objects in the quiet storage rooms, I get these vivid episodes where it feels like I’m back there again—the street, the grip on my arm—so real I lose track of where I am for a moment. My head feels foggy afterwards, like my thoughts are wading through mud.

I used to take pride in my career, but now even getting a new exhibit installed feels hollow. I catch myself thinking none of it really matters, and when colleagues congratulate me, it barely registers. I also can’t shake this sense of humiliation about what happened, like it somehow says something shameful about me, even though I know that’s irrational. Part of me still feels angry and keeps replaying how the police handled it, blaming them for not preventing it, even though another part of me knows that’s not entirely fair.
D018-D001_h003.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

D018-D001_h004.question:
I’ve always been “that scattered kid,” even in primary school. Teachers used to write on my reports that I was bright but never finished anything, always daydreaming or talking, forgetting homework, losing books. It’s kind of followed me my whole life—at work now, I can be in a meeting and my mind just drifts off in the middle of someone’s sentence, or I’ll read the same email three times and still miss a key point. Even watching a show with my husband, I realize I’ve zoned out and have no idea what’s going on.

The trauma is newer. Since that car accident two years ago, I get these sudden, vivid flashes of it—like I’m back there for a few seconds. I’m constantly on edge, tense, like something bad is about to happen. If someone brushes past me unexpectedly, I jump out of my skin. I keep replaying how it happened and, honestly, I’ve put a lot of the blame on the other driver and even my husband for pushing me to drive that day. 

What’s strange is, I don’t feel much when I achieve things anymore—promotions, project wins—they barely register emotionally. I just move on to the next fire to put out.
D018-D001_h004.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

D018-D001_h005.question:
I’ve always been pretty scattered, even as a kid. My mom used to joke that I’d start five things and finish none—teachers wrote “bright but doesn’t focus” on my report cards. I remember in elementary school staring out the window instead of doing math, losing track of instructions, and getting in trouble for talking and fidgeting. That hasn’t really changed; in my work now, I’ll be in the middle of writing code and suddenly realize I’ve opened three unrelated tabs and forgotten what I was doing. I miss details in emails, double‑book meetings, and I can’t sit through long calls without pacing or clicking a pen.

The attention stuff has always been there, long before the accident a few years ago. Since that, certain things set me off physically—like hearing screeching tires or smelling gasoline makes my heart race and my palms sweat. I get really jumpy if someone taps me on the shoulder unexpectedly. I’ve also become angrier; it’s like I’m simmering under the surface, snapping more at colleagues and my ex. I catch myself blaming the other driver and even my ex‑wife for pushing me to drive that day, but at the same time I don’t really care about work wins anymore—even big projects landing don’t feel like much. Making basic choices, like what to eat or what to wear, can weirdly paralyze me; I’ll stand in front of the fridge or closet way too long, unable to decide.
D018-D001_h005.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

D018-D001_h006.question:
I’ve always been a bit “scattered,” even as a kid. My teachers used to write on my report cards that I couldn’t sit still, talked too much, daydreamed, and never finished my work. That same pattern followed me through nursing school and on the wards—forgetting steps, misplacing charts, needing people to repeat things because my mind would drift off.

The accident at the hospital about ten years ago made everything worse. I know something terrible happened on that shift—I remember alarms, people shouting—but there are big blank spots. I can’t recall most of what actually happened, almost like that whole night has been erased. When anything reminds me of it—certain beeping sounds, or even walking past a hospital—I get this intense wave of panic and dread. I try very hard not to think about it at all, push the memories away.

Since then I jump at the slightest movement in my peripheral vision; if someone comes into a room too quickly, I practically leap out of my chair. I also find myself snapping at my daughter and grandkids over small things, yelling before I even realize it. And it bothers me that I feel kind of numb with them sometimes, like I’m going through the motions instead of really feeling close.
D018-D001_h006.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D001_h007.question:
I sell houses, so my job is all over the place, and honestly my mind has always matched that chaos. Even as a kid, teachers told my parents I “lived in my own world,” couldn’t sit still, always blurting things out, starting projects and never finishing. That hasn’t really changed—I still lose track of conversations with clients mid-sentence, misplace paperwork constantly, and I’ll interrupt people without meaning to. I double-book showings, forget appointments I just wrote down, and my husband jokes that being around me is like living with a tornado. I feel restless all the time, like I need to be moving or doing three things at once.

The trauma stuff came later, after an incident a few years ago when I was showing a property and something happened there. The memory is weirdly blank; I can’t piece most of it together. Since then, I have these awful dreams tied to that day and I steer clear of that neighborhood and certain types of properties. I jump out of my skin at loud noises, and I’ve thrown things or shoved my husband when I get overwhelmed. Lately I feel…muted toward him and the kids, like there’s a wall between us and I can’t feel what I know I’m supposed to.
D018-D001_h007.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D001_h008.question:
I’m here mainly because I’ve never really been able to focus, and it’s catching up with me now that I’m retired. My wife keeps saying I “live in half-finished sentences.” I’ll start paying bills, then wander off to check the kettle, then see the mail and forget completely what I was doing. It’s always been like this, even back in primary school—teachers complained I was daydreaming, fidgeting, talking out of turn, blurting answers. I just thought I was “restless,” but it was there long before anything bad happened in my life.

Since my time in the service, I’ve had these awful dreams—same scenes, same feeling of terror—and I try not to think about that period at all. Sometimes I remember tiny details vividly and other parts are just blank, like pieces of film missing. During the day I can feel oddly shut down, like I’m going through the motions and can’t feel much of anything.

I do get jumpy if someone comes up from behind quickly, and once in a while I’ve lashed out or slammed things when I’m on edge, which embarrasses me. But the trouble sitting still, staying on task, and keeping my mind on one thing has been there since I was a boy.
D018-D001_h008.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D001_h009.question:
I work on roofs all day, wiring solar panels, and it’s getting harder to keep it together. I’ve had trouble focusing for as long as I can remember, even back in grade school — teachers always said I was “daydreaming” or “bouncing off the walls.” I’d start assignments, then drift off or get up and wander. That same thing is still happening at work now: I’ll start a job, then catch myself halfway through another task, forgetting what I was doing. My mind jumps around constantly, and I talk over people and blurt things out before I think.

About a year ago I was on a site where there was a really bad accident. I honestly can’t remember most of it — just bits and pieces, like flashing images. Since then I’ve been having these awful dreams that feel tied to that day, but I can’t really say what exactly happened in them. I try not to think about it at all. My wife says I snap and yell over small stuff now, and if someone taps me on the shoulder unexpectedly, I almost jump out of my skin. Even when good things happen, like my kids being excited to see me, it’s like I’m numb and can’t really feel happy.
D018-D001_h009.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D001_h010.question:

My mind jumps around, and I have to reread instructions over and over.

The accident on site a couple years back made things worse in a different way. Sometimes, out of nowhere, it’s like I’m back there—I can smell the dust and hear the screaming, and for a few seconds I’m not in the present at all. I avoid that part of the yard and even dodge talking about it with the guys. I remember some parts of that day crystal clear and other parts are just blank.

Since then, I snap at my wife and kids over nothing, yelling before I even realize it. If something drops loudly, my heart starts racing and my hands shake, and it takes a long while before I feel normal again. Even when good stuff happens—like my son’s game or a raise—I feel kind of flat, like I’m watching it from a distance, not really happy.
